input.question: If the sensation of pain is there to tell us we have been damaged, why are serious injuries usually accompanied by such crippling pain that we are unable to move/do anything about the injury?
input.ground_truth: The pain is usually there to keep you from moving and making things worse. In an actual emergency the body releasing pain-blocking chemicals that will allow you to ignore the pain so you can do what you need to in order to survive.

response.prediction:
Okay, imagine you have a toy robot. If your robot bumps into something and gets a little scratch, it makes a tiny beep sound to tell you, "Hey, something's not right!"

But if your robot gets a really big scratch or breaks a part, it makes a super loud, scary noise. That super loud noise is like the pain you feel when you get hurt really badly.

The reason for the loud noise (or the strong pain) is because your body is trying super hard to tell you, "STOP! Something very important is broken or hurt! You need help right now!"

If you didn't feel that strong pain, you might not know how serious it is, and you might keep using that part of your body and make the injury even worse. So, your body gives you a lot of pain to protect you and tell you to stop and take care of yourself.
